$comment: How to score the writing: the rubrics of the writing part of the unit checks of the eight English writing units (Wave 4, phase 1, 2026-11-19; revised after the writing review en.review-1119-write, the same day). Per unit: the type whose checkWrite(args, ctx) gives the tasks and its level, the task of form A and of form B (two different prompts of the same kind, ids of that hook), the writing lines of the form (Kindergarten: a box to draw in and three rows), the direction of the part, an optional teacherNote (one sentence the teacher pages print under the guide's lead), and three to five points. Each point is scored 0 (notYet), 1 (nearly) or 2 (secure): `shows` is what a teacher can see on the page, written so that every common piece of the grade fits exactly one level, `example` is a piece a child of the grade writes for form A's task and shows its own level only, `next` is a concrete step for a child at that level in this unit (a lesson by its title, or a worksheet of the unit by its title and level). A point asks only what the grade's standard asks. Kindergarten and Grade 1 examples keep the child's sounded-out spelling.

k-draw-and-write-opinions-facts-and-stor.instruction: Your teacher reads the words at the top. Draw your favorite in the big dotted box. Show who is with you, where you are, or what you do with it. Then write what you like best and why.
k-draw-and-write-opinions-facts-and-stor.teacherNote: The writing part asks for an opinion piece in both forms; the unit's other kinds of writing are checked in part 2 (which sentences tell facts about the thing in the picture) and part 3 (putting the events of a small moment in order).

notYet.shows: No favorite is named in words: only the topic word, a list, or letters the child cannot read back as a choice.
notYet.example: fud

nearly.shows: The favorite is named with one word or a label, not in a sentence.
nearly.example: pitsu

secure.shows: A sentence that tells what the child likes (My favorite ___ is ___, I like ___ best, or I like ___.).
secure.example: My favrit fud is pitsu.

next.notYet: Lesson 1, My favorite and why: an opinion: say "My favorite food is ..." aloud first, then write it on the easier page of My Favorite and Why (Level 1), which prints "My favorite" and "is".
next.nearly: My Favorite and Why, Level 1: write the favorite after the printed word "is", so the label becomes a sentence.
next.secure: My Favorite and Why, Level 2: write a reason after the printed word "because" (telling why comes with Grade 1, so this check does not score it).

points.name: The picture shows the favorite and a detail

notYet.shows: No drawing, or a drawing of something the words do not name.
notYet.example: [a drawing of a house] My favrit fud is pitsu.

nearly.shows: The drawing shows the favorite the words name, and nothing more.
nearly.example: [one slice of pizza] My favrit fud is pitsu.

secure.shows: The drawing shows the favorite and one more detail: who is there, where it is, or what is happening.
secure.example: [a girl eating a slice of pizza at a table] My favrit fud is pitsu.

next.notYet: Lesson 2, Teach a fact: draw, label, and write: draw the thing the words name, then write about it.
next.nearly: Lesson 4, Author's chair: a friend asks, I add: add to the drawing the detail a friend asks about (who, where, or what is happening).
next.secure: Facts and Labels, Level 2: write the labels of two parts of a picture.

points.name: Letters for sounds, spaces, a capital, and an end mark

notYet.shows: Letters that do not stand for the sounds of the words (random letters, or the same letters again and again), so the words cannot be read back.
notYet.example: OTBSAEOM

nearly.shows: Letters for the sounds of the words, at least the first sound of most words, but not all that Secure asks: some words have only their first letter, or the spaces, the capital at the start, or the end mark are missing.
nearly.example: M f f i p

secure.shows: A letter for most sounds in each word, spaces between words, a capital at the start, and an end mark.
secure.example: My favrit fud is pitsu.

next.notYet: Lesson 3, My Small Moment, Level 1: write the one short frame "I ___", saying the word slowly and writing a letter for each sound you hear.
next.nearly: My Favorite and Why, Level 2: say each word slowly and write a letter for each sound, leave a finger space after each word, then check the capital and the period.
next.secure: Lesson 4, Author’s Chair, Level 3: write the added detail as a sentence with a capital and a period.

g1-writing-stories-opinions-and-facts.instruction: Your teacher reads the question. Write your opinion: name your topic, tell what you think and why, and end your piece.
g1-writing-stories-opinions-and-facts.teacherNote: The writing part asks for an opinion piece in both forms; the unit's other kinds of writing are checked in part 1 (putting the events of a true story in order) and part 3 (finding the closing sentence of a fact file).

points.name: Names the topic and the opinion

notYet.shows: No opinion: the writing tells about the topic but never says what the child thinks is best.
notYet.example: In fal the leefs fall down.

nearly.shows: An opinion whose topic is not clear: the piece never names what is the best (I think it is the best.).
nearly.example: I think it is the best.

secure.shows: The opinion names its topic, in a sentence of its own or inside the opinion (This is about the best season., or I think fall is the best season.).
secure.example: I think fall is the best season.

next.notYet: Lesson 2, My opinion and a reason: on Opinion or Reason?, sort each sentence under opinion or reason.
next.nearly: Write My Opinion, Level 1: the frame "This is about the best ___." starts the piece with its topic.
next.secure: Lesson 3, All about a topic: facts and a closing: name a topic and keep every sentence on it.

notYet.shows: No reason: the opinion stands alone.
notYet.example: I think fall is the best season.

nearly.shows: A reason that does not tell why: it says the opinion again, or only "I like it".
nearly.example: I think fall is the best becuz I like fall.

secure.shows: A reason that tells why the opinion is true, after because or in a sentence of its own.
secure.example: Fall is the best. You can jump in the leevs.

next.notYet: Opinion or Reason?, part 3: circle because and underline the reason after it; then add a reason to the child's own opinion.
next.nearly: Opinion or Reason?, part 2: match each opinion to the reason that tells why.
next.secure: Write My Opinion, Level 3: write a second reason on the open rows.

notYet.shows: No ending: the piece stops after the reason.
notYet.example: I think fall is the best becuz the leevs turn red.

nearly.shows: An ending that does not go back to the opinion (The end. That is all.).
nearly.example: The end.

secure.shows: A closing that goes back to the opinion: it says the opinion again, in the same or in new words, or speaks to the reader about it (I hope you like fall too!).
secure.example: That is why I pick fall!

next.notYet: Lesson 3, Facts and a Closing: circle the closing sentence among the endings.
next.nearly: Write My Opinion, Level 1: the frame "That is why I pick ___." shows an ending that goes back to the opinion.
next.secure: Lesson 4, Revise and edit with a checklist: check I wrote an ending with a partner.

notYet.shows: Most sentences have no capital at the start or no end mark.
notYet.example: this is about the best season i think fall is the best

nearly.shows: Some sentences start with a capital and end with an end mark and some do not, or I is written small.
nearly.example: This is about the best season. i think fall is the best becuz the leevs turn red

secure.shows: Every sentence starts with a capital and ends with an end mark, and I is a capital.
secure.example: This is about the best season. I think fall is the best because the leevs turn red. That is why I pick fall.

next.notYet: Lesson 4, Edit and Add a Detail, Level 1: fix a small letter at the start and a missing period.
next.nearly: Edit and Add a Detail, Level 2: it adds the small i to fix.
next.secure: Revise with a Checklist: check capitals and end marks in the Me box, then a partner checks them.

g2-writing-stories.instruction: Write a true story about this idea. Tell what happened in order with time words, one thing you thought or felt, and how it ended.

points.name: Events in order with time words

notYet.shows: One event, or events that are not in a clear order.
notYet.example: I helped Dev pick up his crayons.

nearly.shows: Two or more events in order, with no time words, only one, or the same one each time (then, then, then).
nearly.example: First I saw Dev drop his crayons. Then I picked them up. Then we put them away.

secure.shows: Three or more events in order, with a different time word for each (first, next, after that, later, last).
secure.example: First, I saw Dev drop his crayons. Next, I picked them up. After that, we sorted the colors.

next.notYet: Lesson 3, Plan Your True Story, Level 1: write each event after First, I / Next, I / Last, I.
next.nearly: Parts of a True Story: circle the three words that tell the order, then use a different one for each event.
next.secure: Lesson 4, Revise with a Partner: add a detail where the partner asks a question.

notYet.shows: No thought or feeling: only what happened.
notYet.example: I picked up the crayons. I put them in the box.

nearly.shows: A feeling or thought named in a word or two that does not say what it is about (I was happy.).
nearly.example: I was happy.

secure.shows: A thought or a feeling and what it is about.
secure.example: I felt proud that I helped Dev.

next.notYet: Parts of a True Story: underline the sentence that tells a thought or a feeling.
next.nearly: Draft Your True Story, Level 1: the frame At the end, I felt ___ asks for the feeling and its reason.
next.secure: Draft Your True Story, Level 3: tell one thing you saw or heard, too.

points.name: An ending that closes the story

notYet.shows: No ending: the last sentence tells one more event, or the story ends with The end.
notYet.example: After that, we sorted the colors. The end.

nearly.shows: An ending that starts something new or tells the beginning again.
nearly.example: At the end, we went to lunch and had pizza.

secure.shows: A sentence after the last event that tells how it turned out or how the child felt at the end (a feeling here may earn the feeling point too).
secure.example: In the end, all of Dev's crayons were back in his box.

next.notYet: Parts of a True Story, Level 1: circle the sentence that ends the story among three.
next.nearly: Parts of a True Story, Level 2: tell the ending from a sentence that starts something new.
next.secure: Revise with a Partner: the partner asks how it turned out, and the child adds the answer to the ending.

notYet.shows: Many sentences run together with no end mark, or start with a small letter.
notYet.example: first i saw dev drop his crayons and i picked them up and he said thanks

nearly.shows: Most sentences start with a capital and end with an end mark, but a name or I is small or one or two end marks are missing.
nearly.example: First, I saw dev drop his crayons. Next, I picked them up he said thanks.

secure.shows: Every sentence starts with a capital and ends with an end mark; names and I have capitals.
secure.example: First, I saw Dev drop his crayons. Next, I picked them up. He said thanks.

next.notYet: Lesson 4, Edit a Story, Level 1: fix two capital letters and two end marks.
next.nearly: Edit a Story, Level 2: find the name in small letters and the missing end marks.
next.secure: Revise with a Partner: check capitals and end marks together with the checklist.

g2-writing-to-inform.instruction: Write an informative piece about the topic. Use the facts. Start with a topic sentence, tell facts with linking words, tell in your own words what one word means, and end with a closing sentence.

notYet.shows: No topic sentence: the piece starts with a fact.
notYet.example: Foxes have bushy tails.

nearly.shows: The topic is named in a word or a title, not in a sentence.
nearly.example: Foxes

secure.shows: A first sentence that names the topic and tells what the piece is about.
secure.example: Here are some facts about foxes.

next.notYet: Lesson 2, Parts of an Informative Piece: underline the topic sentence of the piece.
next.nearly: Plan Your Informative Piece, Level 1: the frame Here are some facts about ___. starts the plan.
next.secure: Lesson 3, Draft Your Informative Piece, Level 3: write the topic sentence on an open line.

notYet.shows: One fact, or facts that are not about the topic.
notYet.example: Foxes have bushy tails. I like foxes.

nearly.shows: Two or more facts about the topic, with no linking word or only one (also, another, and).
nearly.example: Foxes have bushy tails and pointed ears.

secure.shows: Three or more facts about the topic, joined by two or more linking words.
secure.example: Foxes have bushy tails and pointed ears. They can also hear very well.

next.notYet: Parts of an Informative Piece: cross out the sentence that does not belong.
next.nearly: Lesson 3, Closing Sentences and Linking Words: circle the linking word that fits each blank.
next.secure: Lesson 4, Research with two books: a class report: take notes from two books.

notYet.shows: No word with its meaning.
notYet.example: Foxes eat berries. Now you know about foxes.

nearly.shows: A word and its meaning copied from the facts box as printed (A baby fox is called a kit.), or a meaning that is wrong or unclear.
nearly.example: A baby fox is called a kit.

secure.shows: A word and its meaning in the child's own sentence (A ___ is ___.).
secure.example: A kit is a baby fox.

next.notYet: Closing Sentences and Linking Words, Level 1: read the sentence and finish the definition.
next.nearly: Closing Sentences and Linking Words, Level 3: write a definition with the frame A ___ is ___.
next.secure: Draft Your Informative Piece, Level 3: write the definition of another word from the facts in the piece.

notYet.shows: No closing: the piece stops after a fact.
notYet.example: They also eat berries.

nearly.shows: A closing that is the topic sentence again word for word, or The end.
nearly.example: Here are some facts about foxes.

secure.shows: A closing sentence that ends the piece.
secure.example: Now you know about foxes.

next.notYet: Closing Sentences and Linking Words: circle the closing sentence that fits the piece.
next.nearly: Closing Sentences and Linking Words, Level 2: tell the closing from the topic sentence again.
next.secure: Draft Your Informative Piece, Level 3: end with a closing of the child's own words.

notYet.shows: Many sentences run together with no end mark, or start with a small letter.
notYet.example: foxes have bushy tails they eat mice and berries

nearly.shows: Most sentences start with a capital and end with an end mark; one or two do not.
nearly.example: Here are some facts about foxes. Foxes have bushy tails they eat mice.

secure.shows: Every sentence starts with a capital and ends with an end mark.
secure.example: Here are some facts about foxes. Foxes have bushy tails. They eat mice.

next.notYet: Draft Your Informative Piece, Level 1: the frames start each sentence; the child adds the end mark.
next.nearly: Draft Your Informative Piece: read each sentence aloud and check its capital and end mark with the check list.
next.secure: Write Your Part of the Class Report: check every sentence with the check list.

g2-opinion-writing-and-letters.instruction: Write an opinion piece about the question. Tell your opinion, give two or three reasons with linking words (because, and, also, another reason), and end with a closing sentence.

points.name: An opinion that names the topic

notYet.shows: No opinion: the piece tells about the topic but never says what the child thinks.
notYet.example: At recess we play tag and four square.

nearly.shows: An opinion that names nothing: neither the choice nor the topic (I think it is the best.).
nearly.example: I think it is the best.

secure.shows: An opinion sentence that names the choice or the topic (I think tag is the best., or I think tag is the best game to play at recess.).
secure.example: I think tag is the best game to play at recess.

next.notYet: Lesson 1, Parts of an Opinion Piece: find the opinion among the sentences.
next.nearly: Plan Your Opinion Piece, Level 1: the frame I think ___ is the best. holds the topic.
next.secure: Lesson 2, Revise Your Opinion Piece: add a reason with a linking word.

notYet.shows: No reason, or only reasons that do not tell why.
notYet.example: I think tag is the best game to play at recess. We play it a lot.

nearly.shows: One reason that tells why.
nearly.example: I think tag is the best game because you run a lot.

secure.shows: Two or three reasons that tell why.
secure.example: I think tag is the best game because you run a lot. Also, all my friends can play.

next.notYet: Revise Your Opinion Piece, Level 2: circle the sentence that is a reason (not a fact that does not tell why).
next.nearly: Plan Your Opinion Piece, Level 2: plan a second reason after also.
next.secure: Plan Your Opinion Piece, Level 3: plan three reasons in one box.

notYet.shows: No linking word or phrase: the reasons stand as separate sentences with nothing joining them.
notYet.example: I think tag is the best game. You run a lot. Friends can play.

nearly.shows: One linking word or phrase, used once or again and again (because, because).
nearly.example: I think tag is the best game because you run a lot. Friends can play.

secure.shows: Two or more different linking words or phrases (because, and, also, another reason).
secure.example: I think tag is the best game because you run a lot. Also, all my friends can play, and it is easy to learn.

next.notYet: Parts of an Opinion Piece, part 3: circle because, also, or and in each gap.
next.nearly: Parts of an Opinion Piece: find the reason that starts with also and use also for the second reason.
next.secure: Write Your Opinion Piece, Level 3: write each reason with a different linking word (because, also, and).

notYet.shows: No closing, or The end.
notYet.example: Also, all my friends can play. The end.

nearly.shows: The opinion copied word for word as the last sentence.
nearly.example: I think tag is the best game to play at recess.

secure.shows: A closing sentence that ends the piece: the opinion said again in new words, or a sentence that speaks to the reader (Come play tag with us!).
secure.example: That is why tag is so much fun.

next.notYet: Revise Your Opinion Piece, Level 1: circle the closing that says the opinion in new words.
next.nearly: Revise Your Opinion Piece, Level 1: tell the closing in new words from the opinion copied.
next.secure: Revise Your Opinion Piece, Level 3: write a closing of the child's own that says the opinion in new words.

notYet.shows: Many sentences run together with no end mark, or start with a small letter.
notYet.example: i think tag is the best game because you run a lot also my friends can play

nearly.shows: Most sentences start with a capital and end with an end mark; one or two do not, or I is small.
nearly.example: I think tag is the best game because you run a lot. also, my friends can play

secure.shows: Every sentence starts with a capital and ends with an end mark; I and names have capitals.
secure.example: I think tag is the best game because you run a lot. Also, my friends can play.

next.notYet: Revise Your Opinion Piece: read the piece to a partner and check each sentence's capital and end mark.
next.nearly: Lesson 4, Special Names: Write the Capital Letters: write sentences again with their capitals.
next.secure: Special Names: Find the Capital Letters, Level 3: holidays, places, and product names.

g3-opinion-writing.instruction: Write an opinion piece about the question. Introduce the topic, state your opinion, give two or more reasons with a fact or an example, join them with linking words, and end with a concluding statement.

notYet.shows: No clear opinion: the piece tells about the choices but never picks one.
notYet.example: A farm has animals. A zoo has animals too. A museum has old things.

nearly.shows: An opinion with no introduction: the piece starts with I think.
nearly.example: I think the zoo is the best field trip.

secure.shows: A sentence that introduces the topic, then the opinion.
secure.example: Have you ever thought about where our class should go on a field trip? I think the zoo is the best field trip.

next.notYet: Lesson 1, Opinions and Reasons: underline the opinion of the piece.
next.nearly: Plan Your Opinion Piece, Level 1: the frame Have you ever thought about ___? starts the introduction.
next.secure: Plan Your Opinion Piece, Level 3: plan an introduction of the child's own.

notYet.shows: No reason, or reasons that do not support the opinion.
notYet.example: I think the zoo is the best. I went to a farm once.

nearly.shows: One reason that supports the opinion, or two or more with no fact or example.
nearly.example: One reason is that you see wild animals. Another reason is that it is fun.

secure.shows: Two or more reasons that support the opinion, and at least one of them has a fact or an example.
secure.example: One reason is that you see wild animals. For example, you can watch a lion eat. Another reason is that you learn where animals live.

next.notYet: Opinions and Reasons: circle the number of each reason in the piece.
next.nearly: Plan Your Opinion Piece, Level 2: plan a fact or an example under a reason.
next.secure: Lesson 3, Find the Conclusion: tell a new reason from a conclusion.

notYet.shows: No linking word or phrase joins the opinion and the reasons.
notYet.example: The zoo is the best. You see lions. You see bears.

nearly.shows: One linking word or phrase, used once or again and again (because, because).
nearly.example: I think the zoo is best because you see lions. I like it because you see bears.

secure.shows: Two or more different linking words or phrases from because, since, therefore, for example, and another reason (“and” and “also” do not count here).
secure.example: I think the zoo is best since you see wild animals. For example, you can watch a lion eat.

next.notYet: Lesson 2, Choose the Linking Word, Level 1: circle the word that fits each gap.
next.nearly: Choose the Linking Word, Level 2: tell because and since from therefore and for example.
next.secure: Choose the Linking Word, Level 3: join two sentences starting with Since.

notYet.shows: No conclusion, or The end. or That is all.
notYet.example: You learn where animals live. The end.

nearly.shows: The opinion copied word for word.
nearly.example: I think the zoo is the best field trip.

secure.shows: A concluding statement that ends the piece: the opinion in new words, or a sentence that sums up the reasons or asks the reader to agree.
secure.example: That is why no field trip beats a day at the zoo.

next.notYet: Lesson 3, Find the Conclusion, Level 1: circle the concluding statement of each piece.
next.nearly: Write a Conclusion, Level 1: the frame "That is why ___." says the opinion in new words.
next.secure: Write a Conclusion, Level 3: write a conclusion with words from the word bank.

points.name: Capitals, end marks, and the comma after For example

notYet.shows: Three or more sentences start with a small letter or have no end mark.
notYet.example: i think the zoo is the best you see lions for example you can watch a lion eat

nearly.shows: One or two sentences miss a capital or an end mark, or For example has no comma after it.
nearly.example: I think the zoo is the best. For example you can watch a lion eat.

secure.shows: Every sentence starts with a capital and ends with an end mark, and For example, where it is used, has a comma after it.
secure.example: I think the zoo is the best. For example, you can watch a lion eat.

next.notYet: Lesson 4, Edit an Opinion Paragraph, Level 1: fix the capitals and end marks.
next.nearly: Edit an Opinion Paragraph, Level 2: it adds the missing comma after For example.
next.secure: Revise Your Opinion Piece: check the piece in the Me boxes, then a partner checks it.

g3-informative-writing-and-research.instruction: Write an informative piece about the topic from the notes. Introduce the topic, group the facts in parts, use facts, a definition, and details, and end with a concluding sentence.

notYet.shows: No introduction: the piece starts with a fact from the notes.
notYet.example: Beavers have teeth that keep growing.

nearly.shows: The topic only as a title or a single word, not in a sentence.
nearly.example: Beavers

secure.shows: A sentence that introduces the topic (This is about beavers., a question to the reader, or a sentence that tells what the reader will learn).
secure.example: This report is about beavers and how they live.

next.notYet: Lesson 2, Introductions and Groups: circle the sentence that introduces the topic best.
next.nearly: Introductions and Groups: tell an introduction from a detail.
next.secure: Plan Informative Writing, Level 3: write the introduction of the child's own.

notYet.shows: The facts are in no order: one part jumps between body, food, and home.
notYet.example: Beavers eat bark. They have flat tails. They eat water lilies. They build lodges.

nearly.shows: Most facts are grouped, but one part mixes in a fact of another heading.
nearly.example: Beavers eat bark and twigs. They eat water lilies. They have flat tails.

secure.shows: Facts grouped in parts by heading (a part for body, one for food, one for home).
secure.example: Beavers eat tree bark and twigs. In summer, they also eat water lilies. Beavers build a home called a lodge.

next.notYet: Lesson 1, Choose and Sort Notes: sort the notes under their headings.
next.nearly: Introductions and Groups: write each group's heading from the box.
next.secure: Lesson 4, Notes from Two Sources: sort notes by category from two sources.

notYet.shows: The notes copied as a list, not in sentences.
notYet.example: teeth keep growing, flat tail, eat bark

nearly.shows: Facts in sentences, but no definition, or no detail (a detail is a sentence that tells more about the fact just before it).
nearly.example: Beavers build lodges. Beavers build dams.

secure.shows: Facts in sentences, with a definition and a detail: a sentence that tells more about the fact just before it (the lodge has an underwater door).
secure.example: Beavers build a home called a lodge. A lodge is a home made of sticks and mud. It has an underwater door.

next.notYet: Lesson 1, Take Notes and Sort Them: turn each note into a sentence.
next.nearly: Lesson 3, Fact, Definition, or Detail?: mark each sentence after the fact of a part.
next.secure: Develop Your Topic, Level 3: write the definition with the frame ___, or ___,

notYet.shows: No concluding sentence: the piece stops after a fact.
notYet.example: It has an underwater door.

nearly.shows: The introduction copied word for word as the last sentence.
nearly.example: This report is about beavers and how they live.

secure.shows: A concluding sentence that ends the piece in new words.
secure.example: Now you know why beavers are such busy builders.

next.notYet: Develop Your Topic, Level 1: the frame for the concluding sentence starts it.
next.nearly: Develop Your Topic: write the concluding sentence about what the reader learned.
next.secure: Lesson 4, Write a Research Report: end the report with a concluding sentence.

points.name: Capitals, end marks, and commas in a list

notYet.shows: Three or more sentences start with a small letter or have no end mark.
notYet.example: beavers eat bark they build lodges they have flat tails

nearly.shows: One or two sentences miss a capital or an end mark, or a list of three or more things has no commas.
nearly.example: Beavers eat bark twigs and water lilies.

secure.shows: Every sentence starts with a capital and ends with an end mark, and a list of three or more things, where there is one, has its commas.
secure.example: Beavers eat bark, twigs, and water lilies.

next.notYet: Develop Your Topic: read each sentence of the draft aloud and put a capital at its start and an end mark where the voice stops.
next.nearly: Develop Your Topic: find each list of three things in the draft and put a comma after the first two.
next.secure: Lesson 4, Write a Research Report: write the report from the notes with every sentence and list marked the same way.

g3-narrative-writing.instruction: Write a story about the idea. Introduce the characters, the setting, and the problem, tell the events in order with time words, show how a character feels with dialogue and an action, and write an ending that solves the problem and tells how a character feels.

notYet.shows: No narrator or character, or no problem: the story starts in the middle of an event.
notYet.example: It ran under the desk and we looked.

nearly.shows: Characters and a problem, but no setting (where or when).
nearly.example: Mia saw that Nibbles the hamster was not in his cage.

secure.shows: The characters, where and when, and the problem.
secure.example: On Monday morning, Mia saw that Nibbles, our class hamster, was not in his cage.

next.notYet: Lesson 1, The Parts of a Story: circle who is in the story and what goes wrong.
next.nearly: Plan Your Story, Level 1: the starters for characters and setting.
next.secure: Lesson 2, Show Feelings in a Story: show how the characters feel about the problem.

points.name: Events in order with time words

notYet.shows: One event, or events out of order.
notYet.example: We found him. He was gone. We looked in the closet.

nearly.shows: Events in order, with no time words or the same one each time (then, then).
nearly.example: Then we looked under the desks. Then we looked in the closet. Then we found him.

secure.shows: Events in order with different time words (later that day, after a while, finally).
secure.example: First, we looked under the desks. After a while, Ben checked the closet. Finally, we heard a squeak behind the books.

next.notYet: Lesson 3, Time Words in a Story: number the events of a story.
next.nearly: Time Words in a Story: circle the time word that fits each tiny story.
next.secure: Write with Time Words, Level 3: use time words from the word bank.

notYet.shows: No feeling is shown: feelings are only told (She was sad.), or there are none.
notYet.example: Mia was worried.

nearly.shows: A feeling shown by dialogue or by an action, but not by both.
nearly.example: Mia's hands shook.

secure.shows: Dialogue and an action or a thought that show how a character feels.
secure.example: Mia's hands shook. "What if he is lost?" she whispered.

next.notYet: Lesson 2, Show Feelings in a Story, Level 1: circle the sentence that shows the feeling.
next.nearly: Show Feelings in a Story, Level 2: show the feeling with an action, and write a line of dialogue with a said-word from the box.
next.secure: Lesson 4, Choose a More Exact Word: change tired words such as said and went.

notYet.shows: The problem is not solved: the story stops, or ends with The end.
notYet.example: We looked in the closet. The end.

nearly.shows: The problem is solved in a rush, or the ending turns to something new.
nearly.example: Then we found him. Then it was time for lunch.

secure.shows: The problem is solved, and the ending tells how a character feels or what a character thinks.
secure.example: At last, Nibbles was back in his cage, and Mia smiled because he was safe.

next.notYet: Plan Your Story, Level 1: the starter In the end, plans the ending.
next.nearly: Time Words in a Story: use a time word that ends a story (finally, in the end).
next.secure: Revise for Words That Work: circle three tired words in the story, one of them in the ending, and write the new sentences.

notYet.shows: Three or more sentences run together or have no end mark, or dialogue has no quotation marks.
notYet.example: Mia said where is Nibbles we looked everywhere

nearly.shows: One or two sentences miss a capital or an end mark, or dialogue has quotation marks but its comma or end mark is missing or outside them.
nearly.example: "Where is Nibbles" said Mia.

secure.shows: Every sentence has a capital and an end mark, and dialogue, where there is some, is in quotation marks with its comma or end mark inside.
secure.example: "Where is Nibbles?" asked Mia.

next.notYet: Lesson 2, Quotation Marks in Dialogue, Level 1: circle the sentence that shows the exact words.
next.nearly: Quotation Marks in Dialogue, Level 2: circle the sentence written the right way and write two lines of dialogue.
next.secure: Quotation Marks in Dialogue, Level 3: the speaker comes first (Kim said, "...").

placement-sentence-writing.instruction: Look at the picture. Write two or three sentences about it.
placement-sentence-writing.teacherNote: The writing part of the sentence-writing placement check. Give it to every child, also to a child who stopped earlier on the steps: it is not a step of the ladder. Read the direction and the name of the picture aloud; the child writes alone. Its score places the child in the writing units only: a child with 2 on every point starts at the writing units of Grade 2.

notYet.shows: A word or a list of words, or writing that does not tell about the picture.
notYet.example: horse brown

nearly.shows: One sentence that tells about the picture.
nearly.example: The horse is big.

secure.shows: Two or three sentences, and each one tells something about the picture.
secure.example: The horse is big. It runs fast. It eats hay.

next.notYet: Unit Draw and Write: Opinions, Facts, and Stories (Kindergarten), Lesson 2: Teach a fact: draw, label, and write.
next.nearly: Unit Writing: Stories, Opinions, and Facts (Grade 1), Lesson 3: All about a topic: facts and a closing.
next.secure: Start at Writing Stories (Grade 2), Lesson 1: Write about a picture.

notYet.shows: Groups of words that are not sentences: no one who does something, or nothing that is done.
notYet.example: big horse. run fast.

nearly.shows: Some sentences are complete thoughts, and some are not.
nearly.example: The horse is big. Run fast.

secure.shows: Every sentence is a complete thought.
secure.example: The horse is big. It can run fast.

next.notYet: Unit Draw and Write: Opinions, Facts, and Stories (Kindergarten), Lesson 3: What happened to me: a small moment.
next.nearly: Unit Writing: Stories, Opinions, and Facts (Grade 1), Lesson 1: Write a true story: plan and draft.
next.secure: No extra practice is needed for this point.

notYet.shows: No sentence begins with a capital letter.
notYet.example: the horse is big. it runs fast.

nearly.shows: Some sentences begin with a capital letter, but not all of them.
nearly.example: The horse is big. it runs fast.

secure.shows: Each sentence begins with a capital letter, and the word I is a capital.
secure.example: The horse is big. I like it.

next.notYet: Unit Writing: Stories, Opinions, and Facts (Grade 1), Lesson 4: Revise and edit with a checklist.
next.nearly: Unit Writing Stories (Grade 2), Lesson 4: Revise and edit a story with a checklist.
next.secure: No extra practice is needed for this point.

notYet.shows: No end marks at all.
notYet.example: The horse is big It runs fast

nearly.shows: Some sentences end with a period, a question mark, or an exclamation point; some have none.
nearly.example: The horse is big. It runs fast

secure.shows: Every sentence ends with the right end mark.
secure.example: The horse is big. Can it jump? It runs fast!

next.notYet: Unit Writing: Stories, Opinions, and Facts (Grade 1), Lesson 4: Revise and edit with a checklist.
next.nearly: Unit Writing Stories (Grade 2), Lesson 4: Revise and edit a story with a checklist.
next.secure: No extra practice is needed for this point.
